newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra considers army help for Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra considers army help for Aborigines.

text.p: The Australian government, exasperated with failures to improve Aboriginal living conditions, is looking at sending the army into outback communities to build basic infrastructure.

"It is perhaps an indictment of what has happened in the past but in the end Australians do have a right to basic services such as water and sewerage," Health Minister Michael Wooldridge said, defending the plan.
"A lot of Aboriginal Australians don't have access to that. We have to find a way of doing that whatever way we can," he told reporters.
There was absolutely no doubt that sending in army engineers would raise health standards, he added.

Quoting 1991 figures, Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron said 120 remote communities did not have adequate water supply systems, 134 lacked appropriate sewage disposal and 250 were without electricity.
He complained that Australia had spent an average of A$1 billion a year on Aboriginal welfare yet living conditions were still distressingly poor.
"I find myself asking why, in 1996, and despite that massive investment, the infant mortality in the Aboriginal population is two to three times that of non-Aboriginal children," he said in a speech.
"Life expectancy for indigenous Australians is 16 to 19 years less than for the rest of the population."
Herron is expected to formally announce the army plan on Friday.
"If we could pull it off it would be absolutely fantastic," Wooldridge said.
Aboriginal welfare has been one of the most intractable areas of Australian government policy.

The new conservative government, elected in March, complains that its Labor predecessor threw money at the problem with no noticeable result, partly because of inefficiency within the Aboriginal welfare bureaucracy.
Government sources say the new policy will have a single-minded focus on results, rather than merely funding levels.
